Power System V oltage Stability Evaluation
Considering Renewable Energy With
Correlated V ariabilities
Xiaoyuan Xu , Member , IEEE, Zheng Y an , Mohammad Shahidehpour , Fellow, IEEE, Han Wang,
and Sijie Chen , Member , IEEE
Abstract—Power system operation will encounter numerous
variabilities as the proliferation of renewable energy continues.
Such random events will require the evaluation of corresponding
variables and the assessment of their impacts on the monitoring
and the control of stochastic power systems. In this paper, a global
sensitivity analysis (GSA) method is proposed to perform a pri-
ority ranking of renewable energy variabilities that will affect the
voltage stability of power systems. First, a probabilistic model for
the load margin calculation is presented considering the renewable
power generation. Then, GSA is applied to models with correlated
random input variables and the importance index is designed
for evaluating the impacts of such variables. Next, the stochastic
response surface method is adopted in GSA to improve the
computation efﬁciency of the proposed evaluation method. Finally,
the overall procedure is presented to identify critical variables
that can affect the variability of load margins in voltage stability
analyses. The proposed method is applied to power systems with a
large penetration of renewable power and the inﬂuences of critical
variabilities on voltage stability are analyzed. In this paper, the
proposed method is tested using the IEEE 9-bus and the IEEE
118-bus systems, and its accuracy is compared with those of the
local sensitivity analysis method and the commonly used GSA
methods.
Index Terms —Renewable power, variability, voltage stability,
global sensitivity analysis, stochastic response surface method.

I. I NTRODUCTION
T
HE variability of renewable energy has fundamentally
changed the planning and operation of electric power sys-
tems. Over the last few decades, stochastic power system prob-
lems including the probabilistic load ﬂow and probabilistic small
signal stability have been studied extensively [1]–[6]. Given the
nature of variables, the stochastic methods have aimed at evalu-
ating the uncertain performance of power systems as traditional
deterministic methods cannot fully depict the characteristics of
variable power systems.
The solution of stochastic power system problems with a large
number of random variables will be computationally intractable
as we consider all practical variabilities in power systems [7].
However, it may not be necessary to model all such variabili-
ties, in particular those with a minute impact on power system
operations. Therefore, accurate identiﬁcations of most inﬂuenc-
ing variables will improve the operational efﬁciency of power
systems with less monitoring, and give a better understanding
of relations between input and output variables in solving the
stochastic power system problems.
Sensitivity analysis (SA) is a useful tool to evaluate the
changes in power system outputs as system inputs are varied. SA
provides the information on which input will have the largest ef-
fect on designated system outputs. Broadly speaking, SA meth-
ods can be divided into two categories: local sensitivity analysis
(LSA) and global sensitivity analysis (GSA). LSA usually con-
siders the partial derivative of the output with respect to the
input variable. In [8]–[10], the sensitivities of load margins with
respective to arbitrary parameters were derived. In [11], the ﬁrst
order sensitivity of the available transfer capacity with respect
to power system network variables was described. In [12], a
method based on sensitivity analyses was proposed to rank syn-
chronous generators according to their contributions to angular
and voltage stability. Although LSA has been widely studied in
power system analyses, it also has some shortcomings. Since
power systems models are traditionally nonlinear, LSA would
only be valid for a small region of variabilities in the vicinity
of the power system operating point. Moreover, LSA cannot
consider the correlation between different random variables.
Different from LSA, GSA assesses the impact of a full range
of possible variabilities and takes into account system nonlin-
earities [13]–[14]. The variance-based sensitivity analysis, also
known as the Sobol method, is one of the most popular GSA
methods. By decomposing the variance of the system output
into fractions that can be attributed to inputs or sets of inputs,
it evaluates the impact of input variables. GSA has been ap-
plied to a host of system applications including artiﬁcial neural
networks [15]–[16] and urban water supplies [17]. However,
there have been limited applications of GSA in power systems.
Recently, [7] introduced GSA to power distribution system anal-
yses. In [18], several SA methods including LSA, screening SA
and GSA were compared for identifying critical parameters that
affect the small disturbance stability of a power system.
In previous GSA applications, random input variables were
assumed to be independent and statistical correlations of such
variables were not considered in evaluating the importance of
variabilities. Moreover, several GSA applications to power sys-
tem analyses suffered from signiﬁcant computation burdens
since the Monte Carlo simulation (MCS) was used in global
sensitivity (GS) calculations. Besides, GSA applications to the
static voltage stability assessment of power systems with renew-
able generation were not highlighted.
In this paper, power systems with a signiﬁcant penetration of
renewable generation are studied and an efﬁcient GSA method
is proposed to analyze the inﬂuence of various variabilities on
voltage stability. First, the probabilistic load margin is con-
sidered for power systems with renewable generation, and the
Copula function is adopted to model the correlations among
non-normally distributed variables. Then, GSA for models with
correlated variables is presented, and the importance index is
deﬁned for input variables. Moreover, the stochastic response
surface method (SRSM) is used to establish a surrogate model
of the load margin in order to improve the efﬁciency of calcu-
lating sensitivities. Finally, a procedure is designed to identify
the important variabilities that affect voltage stability. The pro-
posed method is tested using the IEEE 9-bus and IEEE 118-bus
systems, and the results are compared with those of LSA and
other GSA methods to validate the effectiveness of the proposed
method.
II. P ROBABILISTIC VOLTAGESTABILITY ANAL YSIS

power system static voltage stability. The optimization-based

maximizing the load margin while satisfying power ﬂow and
other operating constraints. The solution to the OPF problem
corresponds to the saddle node bifurcation (SNB) point or is
determined by operating constraints of power systems [19]. The
optimization model is given as follows:

IV . PROCEDURE OF VOLTAGESTABILITY GSA
The procedure of the GSA application to voltage stability is
given in Procedure 2. The key steps are using SRSM to establish
surrogate models of load margins and calculating GSs of input
variables.
The proposed GSA method considers correlations among in-
put variables. Moreover, the computation efﬁciency of GSA is
improved tremendously by adopting surrogate models of load
margins for GS calculation.
V. C ASE STUDIES
In this section, the proposed GSA method is tested using the
modiﬁed IEEE 9-bus and IEEE 118-bus systems. In the IEEE
9-bus system, load variabilities are considered, and the accuracy
of the proposed method is compared with those of commonly
used methods to validate the proposed approach. In the IEEE
118-bus system, a large penetration of renewables is consid-
ered. Critical variabilities affecting the power system voltage
stability are identiﬁed, and the impacts of such correlations in
renewable power generation are analyzed on voltage stability.
Programs are developed with Matlab 8.1 on a PC with Inter Core
i5 2.40-GHz CPU and 6GB of RAM. Deterministic load margin
calculation is solved by the interior point nonlinear optimization
method [19].
A. IEEE 9-bus System
In the IEEE 9-bus system, directions of active and reactive
load increase are assumed to follow normal distributions. The
mean values of normal variables are initial loads, and standard
deviations are deﬁned as 10% of the corresponding means. In
this IEEE system, the number of input variables is 6 and 56
points are used to establish the SRSM model. The corresponding
results are compared with the MCS results using a sample size
of 5000.
In Figs. 2 and 3, the probability densities and cumulative
distributions of load margins obtained by SRSM are nearly the
same as those obtained by MCS. If the same sample size is
used in both MCS and SRSM, MCS gives much larger errors.

B. IEEE 118-Bus System
In the original IEEE 118-bus system, the total load is
4,242 MW and the total generation capacity is 9,966.2 MW.
In order to consider the integration of signiﬁcant amount of re-
newable generation, 1,700 MW of conventional generators are
replaced by renewable generators, accounting for 40% of the
total load. The variabilities of renewable generation are consid-
ered and probabilistic models are designed as follows.
The IEEE 118-bus system is divided into four areas of A, B, C
and D, covering buses 1–30, 31–60, 61–90 and 91–118, respec-
tively. Conventional generators at buses 1, 15, 18, 19, 32, 36, 55,
62, 70, 74, 76, 85, 91, 92, 104, 105 and 110 are replaced by wind
farms or PV power stations with the same capacity of 100 MW.
Thus, the renewable generation capacities in areas A, B, C and
D are 400 MW, 300 MW, 500 MW and 500 MW, respectively.
Three types of random input variables (i.e., wind generation, PV
generation and loads) are considered in static voltage stability
analyses. The probability models of the variables are given in
Table III, and the corresponding parameters are obtained from
[26]. Moreover, the renewable units are considered correlated in
the same area and independent in different areas. The Gaussian
Copula is used to describe correlations among renewable power
generation units, and the correlation coefﬁcient of the Gaussian
Copula is set as 0.5.
In Table IV, we deﬁne three systems to analyze the inﬂuence
of renewable power on voltage stability. In S1, conventional
generators, rather than renewable energy units, are considered,
and normally distributed variables are used to describe load
variabilities. In S2, the integration of renewable power gener-
ation is considered and independent non-normal variables are
used to describe renewable power variabilities. In S3, correlated
non-normal variables are used to model the dependence among
renewable energy units.

VI. C ONCLUSION
In this paper, a GSA method is proposed to consider power
system variabilities in the voltage stability evaluation. The pro-
posed method is tested on IEEE 9-bus and IEEE 118-bus sys-
tems, and the results are compared with those of other sensitivity
analysis methods. The following conclusions are drawn:
1) Compared with LSA, the proposed GSA method is more
accurate to consider the relative importance of variables.
2) The results corresponding with the surrogate model of the
load margin established by SRSM are accurate compared
with those of MCS with a large sample size. With the

GSA is signiﬁcantly improved.
3) For power systems with high renewable penetration, the vari-
abilities of renewable power are critical in determining prob-
ability distributions of load margins. Moreover, correlations
among renewable power affect the variability of load margins.
4) Certain variables affect power system operations signiﬁ-
cantly. The proposed GSA method accurately identiﬁes such
variables and thus can be useful for an effective computation
in stochastic power system analyses.
In our future work, we will combine SRSM with the sparse-
adaptive scheme to further improve the computation efﬁciency
of GSA in large-scale power system problems. Besides, we will
adopt the application of the proposed GSA method in heuristic
black-box algorithms such as artiﬁcial neural networks to the
complicated power system problems in which it is difﬁcult to
obtain an analytical closed-form solution.
